title: U.S. History II: Reconstruction to Civil Rights, 1865–1968
objectives: Students will place the major eras of U.S. history from 1865 to 1968 in chronological order and name a defining event of each.
Students will explain causes and effects of Reconstruction, industrialization, immigration, and Progressive Era reform.
Students will describe U.S. involvement in the two world wars, the Great Depression and New Deal, and the Cold War policy of containment.
Students will trace major achievements of the civil rights movement and the federal actions that followed.
Students will answer GED-style questions using timelines, charts, and excerpts from public-domain U.S. government documents.
teach:
Objectives

  • Place the major eras of U.S. history from 1865 to 1968 in order and name one defining event of each.
  • Explain causes and effects of Reconstruction, industrialization, immigration, and Progressive reform.
  • Describe U.S. involvement in World War I and World War II, the Great Depression and the New Deal, and the Cold War policy of containment.
  • Trace the main victories of the civil rights movement and the federal actions that followed.
  • Answer GED-style questions using timelines, charts, tables, and excerpts from public-domain government documents.

Materials

  • Student Lesson (printed or on screen), including the Big Timeline and the immigration chart
  • Study sheet (Notes) for each student
  • Whiteboard or shared screen; sticky notes or index cards with event names for the timeline warm-up
  • Week 6 Social Studies practice set (12 items)

60-Minute Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Put five events in order; quick review of Week 5 (the Civil War)
Direct instruction20Seven eras in seven short stops, using the Big Timeline; worked examples
Guided practice15Four document and data questions worked together
Independent practice15Practice set items 1–8 (finish 9–12 at home)
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding and the exit ticket from the Post Lesson

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Write these five events on the board in scrambled order and ask students to put them in chronological order without notes: the stock market crash; Pearl Harbor is attacked; the 13th Amendment ends slavery; the United States enters World War I; the March on Washington.

Answer: 13th Amendment (1865) → U.S. enters World War I (1917) → stock market crash (1929) → Pearl Harbor (1941) → March on Washington (1963).

Then ask: "Last week ended with the Civil War. What two big questions did the country face in 1865?" Expected: how to bring the Southern states back into the Union, and what freedom and citizenship would mean for about four million formerly enslaved people.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes)

Tell students that the GED does not expect them to memorize hundreds of dates. It expects them to know the order of the eras, the big cause and effect in each, and how to read a document or chart from the period. Keep the Big Timeline in view and spend about three minutes per stop.

Stop 1: Reconstruction (1865–1877)

  • Goal: rebuild the South and define freedom. The 13th (1865), 14th (1868), and 15th (1870) Amendments ended slavery, defined citizenship with equal protection, and banned denying the vote because of race (review from Week 3).
  • The Freedmen's Bureau (1865) set up schools and helped formerly enslaved people find work and family members. Southern states passed Black Codes to limit Black Americans' freedom. Congress responded with the Reconstruction Acts (1867), which placed most of the former Confederacy under military districts.
  • Black men voted and held office; Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black U.S. senator in 1870.
  • End: after the disputed election of 1876, the Compromise of 1877 led to the withdrawal of the last federal troops from the South. Southern states then passed Jim Crow segregation laws and used poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence to block Black voters. Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) allowed "separate but equal."

Stop 2: Industrialization and immigration (about 1865–1900)

  • The first transcontinental railroad was completed at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869. Railroads created a national market. Steel (Andrew Carnegie) and oil (John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil) grew into giant businesses; critics called the most powerful combinations trusts or monopolies.
  • Workers faced long hours, low pay, and dangerous conditions, and many organized labor unions (the American Federation of Labor was founded in 1886). Strikes such as the Pullman Strike (1894) often ended when government sided with employers.
  • Millions of immigrants came for jobs and freedom, many from southern and eastern Europe after 1890. Ellis Island in New York Harbor opened in 1892. Cities grew fast, with crowded tenements.
  • Backlash: the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) was the first major federal law to bar immigrants of a specific nationality. In the 1920s, Congress passed quota laws (1921 and 1924) that sharply limited immigration, especially from southern and eastern Europe, and barred most immigration from Asia.

Stop 3: The Progressive Era (about 1890–1920)

  • Progressives used government to fix problems created by industry and city growth. Journalists called muckrakers exposed abuses: Jacob Riis photographed tenement life (How the Other Half Lives, 1890), Ida Tarbell investigated Standard Oil, and Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle (1906) described filthy meatpacking plants.
  • Results: the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act (both 1906); antitrust lawsuits under the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890), pressed hard by President Theodore Roosevelt; workplace safety laws after the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York killed 146 workers in 1911.
  • Four amendments came out of this era: 16th (income tax, 1913), 17th (voters elect senators, 1913), 18th (Prohibition, 1919), and 19th (women's suffrage, 1920).

Stop 4: World War I (U.S. involvement 1917–1918)

  • War began in Europe in 1914. The United States stayed neutral at first. Causes of U.S. entry: German submarine attacks (the Lusitania was sunk in 1915; Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare in early 1917) and the Zimmermann Telegram, in which Germany proposed an alliance with Mexico.
  • President Woodrow Wilson asked Congress for a declaration of war on April 2, 1917, saying "The world must be made safe for democracy." Congress declared war on April 6, 1917. The armistice took effect on November 11, 1918.
  • After the war, Wilson's Fourteen Points called for a League of Nations, but the U.S. Senate refused to approve the Treaty of Versailles, and the United States never joined the League. Point out the civics link: the Constitution requires two-thirds of the Senate to approve a treaty.

Stop 5: The Great Depression and the New Deal (1929–1941)

  • The stock market crashed in October 1929. Banks failed, businesses closed, and unemployment reached about 25 percent by 1933. Drought and dust storms on the Great Plains (the Dust Bowl) drove many farm families west.
  • President Franklin D. Roosevelt took office on March 4, 1933, and launched the New Deal, often summarized as the "3 Rs": relief for the needy, recovery of the economy, and reform to prevent another collapse.
  • Examples: Civilian Conservation Corps (1933), Tennessee Valley Authority (1933), Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (created by the Banking Act of 1933), Securities and Exchange Commission (1934), Works Progress Administration (1935), Social Security Act (August 14, 1935), and the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938), which set a national minimum wage.
  • The big change: the federal government took on a much larger role in the economy and in people's daily lives.

Stop 6: World War II (U.S. involvement 1941–1945)

  • Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939. The United States stayed officially neutral but sent aid to Britain through Lend-Lease (1941).
  • Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941. Roosevelt asked Congress to declare war the next day, and it did. Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on December 11.
  • Home front: factories switched to war production, unemployment nearly disappeared, and millions of women took industrial jobs. Under Executive Order 9066 (1942), about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, most of them U.S. citizens, were forced from the West Coast into incarceration camps. The Supreme Court upheld the policy in Korematsu v. United States (1944); Congress formally apologized in 1988.
  • End: D-Day (June 6, 1944); Germany surrendered in May 1945; after U.S. atomic bombs struck Hiroshima (August 6) and Nagasaki (August 9), Japan announced its surrender and signed it on September 2, 1945.

Stop 7: The Cold War and the civil rights movement (1945–1968 and beyond)

  • Cold War: a long rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union without direct, large-scale war between them. U.S. policy was containment: stop the spread of communism. Examples: the Truman Doctrine (1947), the Marshall Plan to rebuild Western Europe (1948), the Berlin Airlift (1948–1949), NATO (1949), the Korean War (1950–1953), the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962), and the Vietnam War. The Cold War ended with the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the breakup of the Soviet Union (1991).
  • Civil rights: President Harry Truman ordered equal treatment in the armed forces (Executive Order 9981, 1948). Brown v. Board of Education (1954) ended legal school segregation. Rosa Parks's arrest in December 1955 began the Montgomery Bus Boycott, which lasted more than a year and ended after the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional. Student sit-ins began in Greensboro, North Carolina, in 1960.
  • Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. led nonviolent protest. In his 1963 "Letter from Birmingham Jail," he defended peaceful civil disobedience against unjust laws, and at the March on Washington on August 28, 1963, he described his hope for a nation where people would be judged by their character rather than their race. (Describe these works; do not hand out copies of the text.)
  • Results: the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the 24th Amendment (1964), and, after the 1965 Selma-to-Montgomery marches, the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

Worked Examples

Worked example 1: Cause and effect from a chart. The immigration chart in the Student Lesson shows about 4.1 million immigrants in 1921–1930 and about 0.5 million in 1931–1940. What best explains the drop?

Step 1: Find the size of the change: 4.1 − 0.5 = 3.6 million fewer immigrants. Step 2: Ask what was happening in the 1930s: the Great Depression, when jobs were scarce, and the quota laws of 1921 and 1924, which were already limiting immigration. Step 3: Check the alternatives against the dates. World War II did not involve the United States until December 1941, so it cannot explain the whole decade. Answer: The Great Depression (few jobs) combined with the 1920s quota laws.

Worked example 2: Main idea of a government document. Read: "I ask that the Congress declare that since the unprovoked and dastardly attack by Japan on Sunday, December 7th, 1941, a state of war has existed between the United States and the Japanese Empire." (Franklin D. Roosevelt, address to Congress, December 8, 1941.) What is Roosevelt asking for, and why does he ask Congress?

Step 1: Find the verb of the request: "I ask that the Congress declare." Step 2: Name the request: a declaration of war against Japan. Step 3: Connect to civics: Article I of the Constitution gives Congress, not the President, the power to declare war. Answer: He asks Congress to declare war on Japan because only Congress has that power.

Worked example 3: Sequence and era. Put these in order and name the era of each: the Marshall Plan; the Pure Food and Drug Act; the Freedmen's Bureau; the Works Progress Administration.

Step 1: Assign each to an era. Freedmen's Bureau = Reconstruction (1865). Pure Food and Drug Act = Progressive Era (1906). Works Progress Administration = New Deal (1935). Marshall Plan = Cold War (1948). Step 2: Order the eras. Answer: Freedmen's Bureau → Pure Food and Drug Act → Works Progress Administration → Marshall Plan.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Work these together. For each one, ask students to name the era first, then find the words or numbers that prove the answer.

  1. Read from Wilson's April 2, 1917, address: "We have no selfish ends to serve. We desire no conquest, no dominion." What impression is Wilson trying to give Congress and the public? Answer: that the United States would fight for principles such as democracy, not to gain territory or wealth.
  2. According to the immigration chart, which decade had the most immigrants, and about how many? Answer: 1901–1910, about 8.8 million.
  3. A cartoon shows a giant octopus labeled "Standard Oil" with its arms wrapped around a state capitol and the U.S. Capitol. Which era does it most likely come from, and what is the cartoonist's point? Answer: the Progressive Era (about 1890–1920); the cartoonist believes one powerful company controls government and the economy.
  4. Read from Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965: no "standard, practice, or procedure shall be imposed or applied by any State or political subdivision to deny or abridge the right of any citizen of the United States to vote on account of race or color." Which amendment does this law enforce? Answer: the 15th Amendment (1870). The act's title says it is "to enforce the fifteenth amendment."

Independent Practice (15 minutes)

Students complete practice items 1–8 on their own. Circulate and ask, "Which era is this, and what word or number in the document tells you?" Items 9–12 (the Pearl Harbor address, the Cold War multi-select, a fact-or-opinion item, and a two-document comparison) can be finished at home.

Checks for Understanding

  • "Why did Reconstruction end, and what happened afterward?" Expected: the Compromise of 1877 withdrew federal troops; Southern states passed Jim Crow laws and blocked Black voting.
  • "What did muckrakers do, and give one result." Expected: they exposed problems through journalism; for example, The Jungle led to the Meat Inspection Act and Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906.
  • "Name the 3 Rs of the New Deal and one program." Expected: relief, recovery, reform; for example, Social Security, the WPA, the CCC, or the FDIC.
  • "What was containment? Give one example." Expected: the U.S. policy of stopping the spread of communism; for example, the Marshall Plan, NATO, or the Korean War.
  • "Name two federal laws that came out of the civil rights movement." Expected: the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Mixing up the two world wars. Give an anchor: WWI = Wilson, 1917, "safe for democracy," League of Nations. WWII = Franklin Roosevelt, Pearl Harbor, 1941, atomic bomb. Have students make a two-column chart.

Thinking the Cold War was a direct war between the superpowers. Explain that "cold" means the United States and the Soviet Union never fought each other directly on a large scale; the fighting happened in other places, such as Korea and Vietnam.

Reading a chart as if it proves a cause. The immigration chart shows when numbers changed, not why. Students must bring in outside knowledge (quota laws, the Depression) or a document that states the cause.

Confusing the Progressive Era with the New Deal. Both used government to fix problems. Progressives (about 1890–1920) focused on trusts, food safety, and corruption; the New Deal (1933–1939) responded to the economic collapse of the Great Depression.

Assuming a law ended a problem at once. The 15th Amendment (1870) banned race-based denial of the vote, yet the Voting Rights Act was needed in 1965. Teach students to look for the gap between a law on paper and its enforcement.

Differentiation

Support: Give students a blank seven-row Big Timeline and have them fill in one event and one person for each era as you teach. Pre-teach eight words: Reconstruction, segregation, monopoly, muckraker, quota, depression, containment, civil disobedience. For document questions, have students underline who wrote it and when before reading the question.

Stretch: Ask students to write one paragraph comparing the federal government's role in the Progressive Era and in the New Deal, using one law from each. Or have them compare Executive Order 9981 (1948) and the Voting Rights Act (1965): which branch acted in each, and why might one branch move first?

How This Shows Up on the GED

U.S. history is about 20 percent of the GED Social Studies test, and almost every question gives you a stimulus to read. Expect questions such as:

  • "Based on the excerpt, what was the speaker's main purpose?" (presidential addresses, laws, court opinions)
  • "Which event most directly led to…?" or "What was one effect of…?" (cause and effect)
  • "Which conclusion is supported by the data?" with a chart or table of immigration, unemployment, or wages
  • Drag-and-drop tasks that sort events into eras or place them in order on a timeline
  • Questions that ask which statement is a fact and which is an opinion in a historical account

When discussing segregation, Japanese American incarceration, and immigration restriction, stay with what the documents and the historical record show. Students may connect these topics to their own families; welcome that, and keep the focus on evidence. Do not distribute the texts of Dr. King's speeches or letters, which are not in the public domain; describe them instead.
student:
Why This Matters

About one fifth of the GED Social Studies test is U.S. history, and much of it comes from the hundred years after the Civil War. You will read short pieces of laws and presidential speeches, study charts and timelines, and decide what caused an event or what it led to. You do not need to memorize every date. You do need to know the order of the big eras and the main idea of each.

1. The Big Timeline

EraYearsKey events
Reconstruction1865–187713th, 14th, 15th Amendments; Freedmen's Bureau; federal troops leave the South in 1877
Industrialization and immigrationabout 1865–1900Transcontinental railroad (1869); big business and labor unions; Chinese Exclusion Act (1882); Ellis Island opens (1892)
Progressive Eraabout 1890–1920Muckrakers; Pure Food and Drug Act (1906); 16th–19th Amendments
World War IU.S. in war 1917–1918U.S. declares war (April 1917); armistice (November 11, 1918)
Great Depression and New Deal1929–1941Stock market crash (1929); Franklin D. Roosevelt takes office (1933); Social Security Act (1935)
World War IIU.S. in war 1941–1945Pearl Harbor (December 7, 1941); D-Day (1944); Japan surrenders (1945)
Cold War and civil rights1945–1991NATO (1949); Korean War (1950–1953); Brown v. Board (1954); Civil Rights Act (1964); Voting Rights Act (1965); Soviet Union breaks up (1991)

2. Reconstruction (1865–1877)

After the Civil War, the nation had to bring the Southern states back into the Union and decide what freedom would mean for about four million formerly enslaved people. Three amendments ended slavery (13th), made formerly enslaved people citizens with equal protection of the laws (14th), and banned denying the vote because of race (15th). Black men voted and were elected to office. When federal troops left the South in 1877, Southern states passed Jim Crow laws that segregated Black and white Americans and used poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence to keep Black citizens from voting.

3. Industry, Immigration, and Reform (about 1865–1920)

Railroads, steel, and oil turned the United States into an industrial giant. A few huge companies, called trusts or monopolies, controlled whole industries. Factory workers often worked 60 hours a week in unsafe conditions, so many joined labor unions. Millions of immigrants arrived to fill these jobs, but some Americans wanted to keep certain groups out. The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 was the first major federal law to bar immigrants of one nationality.

The Progressive Era (about 1890–1920) was a response to these problems. Reporters called muckrakers exposed unsafe food, child labor, and corruption. Congress passed food safety laws, broke up some trusts, and added four amendments: the income tax (16th), direct election of senators (17th), Prohibition (18th), and women's right to vote (19th).

Worked example 1: Read a law. The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) said that "the coming of Chinese laborers to the United States be, and the same is hereby, suspended." What did the law do?

Step 1: Find the subject: "the coming of Chinese laborers." Step 2: Find what happens to it: "suspended," which means stopped for a time. Answer: It stopped Chinese workers from immigrating to the United States. (The law set a ten-year ban; later laws extended it until 1943.)

4. Immigration in Numbers

The chart below shows how many immigrants were admitted to the United States in each decade. Notice the high point and the sharp drop.

DecadeImmigrants admitted (millions, rounded)

Source: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Yearbook of Immigration Statistics, Table 1 (decade totals, rounded).

Charts show what changed, not why. To explain a change, match the dates to events you know. The 1911–1920 drop overlaps World War I. The 1921–1930 decline follows the quota laws of 1921 and 1924. The collapse in 1931–1940 matches the Great Depression, when there were few jobs to come for.

5. Two World Wars and a Depression (1914–1945)

World War I began in Europe in 1914. German submarine attacks on ships, including American ones, pushed the United States into the war in April 1917. President Woodrow Wilson told Congress that "the world must be made safe for democracy." The fighting ended on November 11, 1918.

In October 1929 the stock market crashed, and the Great Depression followed. By 1933 about one in four workers had no job. President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal aimed at the "3 Rs": relief (help for the jobless and hungry), recovery (getting the economy working again), and reform (changes so a collapse would not happen again). Social Security, bank deposit insurance, and a minimum wage all date from this time.

World War II began in Europe in 1939. The United States entered after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941. War factories ended the Depression, and millions of women took jobs once held by men. The government also forced about 120,000 Japanese Americans and Japanese immigrants on the West Coast into incarceration camps, an action Congress formally apologized for in 1988. The war ended in 1945.

Worked example 2: Sort into the 3 Rs. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) insures bank deposits so that people do not lose their savings when a bank fails. Is it mainly relief, recovery, or reform?

Step 1: Ask: Does it give direct help now (relief), restart business (recovery), or change the system to prevent a future crisis (reform)? Step 2: Insurance protects savers in future bank failures, a permanent change to the banking system. Answer: reform.

6. The Cold War (1945–1991)

After World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union became rival superpowers. They never fought each other directly on a large scale, which is why it is called a "cold" war. The U.S. policy was containment: keep communism from spreading. The United States gave aid to rebuild Western Europe (the Marshall Plan), formed the NATO military alliance (1949), and fought in Korea (1950–1953) and Vietnam. The Cold War ended when the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991.

7. The Civil Rights Movement (1950s–1960s)

Black Americans and their allies challenged segregation in courts, on buses, at lunch counters, and in the streets. In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Supreme Court ruled that segregated public schools were unconstitutional. Rosa Parks's arrest in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1955 sparked a bus boycott that lasted more than a year. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. led nonviolent protests; at the 1963 March on Washington he spoke of his hope for a nation where people would be judged by their character, not their skin color. Congress then passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which outlawed segregation in public places and job discrimination, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which attacked barriers such as literacy tests.

Worked example 3: Compare two documents. Executive Order 9981 (1948), from President Truman, called for "equality of treatment and opportunity for all persons in the armed services without regard to race, color, religion or national origin." The Voting Rights Act (1965), passed by Congress, banned voting rules used "to deny or abridge the right of any citizen of the United States to vote on account of race or color." How are they alike and different?

Step 1: Alike: both use federal power against racial discrimination. Step 2: Different author: an executive order comes from the President; the Voting Rights Act is a law passed by Congress. Step 3: Different area: the military versus voting. Answer: Both fight discrimination, but one is a presidential order about the armed forces and the other is a law of Congress about voting.

Try It

1. Put in order: New Deal begins; Reconstruction ends; NATO is formed; Progressive food safety laws pass.

Show answer

Reconstruction ends (1877) → food safety laws (1906) → New Deal begins (1933) → NATO is formed (1949).

2. Using the immigration table, how many more immigrants (in millions) arrived in 1901–1910 than in 1891–1900?

Show answer

8.8 − 3.7 = 5.1 million more.

3. The Works Progress Administration hired millions of jobless people to build roads, schools, and parks. Which "R" of the New Deal does this best fit?

Show answer

Relief. It gave immediate jobs and paychecks to unemployed people. (It also helped recovery, but its main purpose was relief.)

4. Why is the Cold War called "cold"?

Show answer

Because the United States and the Soviet Union never fought each other directly in a large-scale war. Their rivalry played out through alliances, an arms race, and wars in other places such as Korea and Vietnam.

5. The 15th Amendment banned denying the vote because of race in 1870. Why was the Voting Rights Act still needed in 1965?

Show answer

Many states got around the 15th Amendment with poll taxes, literacy tests, and intimidation. The Voting Rights Act gave the federal government tools to stop those practices.

Summary of Key Points

  • Reconstruction (1865–1877) brought the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments, but after federal troops left in 1877, Jim Crow laws took away many of those gains.
  • Industrialization created big business, crowded cities, and labor unions, and drew millions of immigrants; the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) and the 1920s quota laws restricted immigration.
  • Progressives (about 1890–1920) used journalism and government to fix problems: food safety laws, trust-busting, and the 16th through 19th Amendments.
  • The United States fought in World War I (1917–1918) and World War II (1941–1945). Between them, the Great Depression led to the New Deal (relief, recovery, reform) and a bigger federal government.
  • The Cold War (1945–1991) was a rivalry with the Soviet Union; the U.S. policy was containment. The civil rights movement won Brown v. Board (1954), the Civil Rights Act (1964), and the Voting Rights Act (1965).

Exit Ticket

1. What event in 1877 marked the end of Reconstruction?

Show answer

The Compromise of 1877, which led to the withdrawal of the last federal troops from the South.

2. Which book exposed conditions in meatpacking plants and helped lead to the food safety laws of 1906?

Show answer

The Jungle, by Upton Sinclair.

3. What event brought the United States into World War II?

Show answer

Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941.

4. Which New Deal law, signed in 1935, created old-age pensions and unemployment insurance?

Show answer

The Social Security Act.

5. Name one example of the U.S. policy of containment.

Show answer

Any one of: the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan, the Berlin Airlift, NATO, the Korean War, or the Vietnam War.

Reflection

  • Many families in the United States have an immigration story. What pushed people to leave their homes, and what pulled them here, in the years shown on this week's chart?
  • The 15th Amendment and the Voting Rights Act were passed almost 100 years apart. What does that gap tell you about how rights are won and protected?
  • Which skill was hardest for you this week: putting events in order, reading a document, or reading a chart? What will you practice?

Test-Taking Strategy: Date the Document First

Before you read a historical document question, look at the source line: who wrote it and when. Place that date on the Big Timeline in your head. Knowing that a speech is from April 1917 or December 1941 tells you which war, which president, and which problems the country faced, and it often rules out two answer choices before you read the document closely.

vocab.def: The period from 1865 to 1877 when the federal government worked to rebuild the South and protect the rights of formerly enslaved people.
vocab.example: The 14th Amendment was ratified during Reconstruction.

vocab.def: State and local laws, mostly in the South, that enforced racial segregation from the late 1800s until the 1960s.
vocab.example: Jim Crow laws required separate waiting rooms for Black and white passengers.

vocab.def: The forced separation of people by race in schools, housing, transportation, and public places.
vocab.example: Brown v. Board of Education ruled school segregation unconstitutional.

vocab.def: The shift from farming and handmade goods to factory production with machines.
vocab.example: Industrialization drew workers from farms to factory cities.

vocab.def: A company or group of companies that controls nearly all of an industry and limits competition.
vocab.example: Standard Oil once refined about 90 percent of the oil in the United States.

vocab.def: An organization of workers who bargain together with employers for better pay, hours, and safety.
vocab.example: The American Federation of Labor was founded in 1886.

vocab.def: A legal limit on the number of immigrants allowed in from a country or region.
vocab.example: The Immigration Act of 1924 set strict quotas based on national origin.

vocab.def: A Progressive Era journalist who exposed corruption and unsafe conditions.
vocab.example: Ida Tarbell was a muckraker who investigated Standard Oil.

vocab.def: A reform period (about 1890 to 1920) when Americans used government to fix problems caused by industry and city growth.
vocab.example: The Pure Food and Drug Act passed during the Progressive Era.

vocab.def: A long, severe drop in economic activity, with high unemployment and many business failures.
vocab.example: Unemployment reached about 25 percent during the Great Depression.

vocab.def: President Franklin D. Roosevelt's programs of the 1930s for relief, recovery, and reform.
vocab.example: Social Security began as part of the New Deal.

vocab.def: The Cold War policy of stopping communism from spreading to more countries.
vocab.example: NATO was formed in 1949 as part of containment.

vocab.def: The rivalry from 1945 to 1991 between the United States and the Soviet Union, fought with alliances, arms races, and wars in other countries rather than direct large-scale combat between the two.
vocab.example: The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 was one of the most dangerous moments of the Cold War.

vocab.def: Peacefully and openly refusing to obey a law one believes is unjust, and accepting the penalty.
vocab.example: Students who sat at whites-only lunch counters in 1960 practiced civil disobedience.

vocab.def: A directive from the President to federal agencies or the armed forces that has the force of law.
vocab.example: Executive Order 9981 (1948) called for equal treatment in the armed forces.

Depression and New Deal1929–1941Crash (Oct. 1929); 25% unemployment (1933); FDR; relief, recovery, reform; Social Security (1935)
World War IIU.S. 1941–1945Pearl Harbor (Dec. 7, 1941); women in war jobs; Japanese American incarceration; D-Day (1944); atomic bombs; surrender (1945)
Cold War1945–1991Containment: Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, NATO, Korea, Vietnam; Cuban Missile Crisis (1962); USSR ends (1991)
Civil rights1948–1968EO 9981 (1948); Brown (1954); Montgomery boycott (1955); March on Washington (1963); Civil Rights Act (1964); Voting Rights Act (1965)

New Deal: the 3 Rs

  • Relief (help now): CCC, WPA
  • Recovery (restart the economy): public works, farm programs
  • Reform (prevent a repeat): FDIC, SEC, Social Security

Immigration (millions per decade)

1881–90: 5.2 • 1901–10: 8.8 (peak) • 1921–30: 4.1 • 1931–40: 0.5 (Depression, quotas)

Key Documents

  • Chinese Exclusion Act (1882): suspended Chinese labor immigration
  • Wilson (Apr. 2, 1917): asks for war on Germany
  • FDR (Dec. 8, 1941): asks Congress to declare war on Japan (only Congress can)
  • EO 9981 (1948): President orders equal treatment in the armed forces
  • Voting Rights Act (1965): law of Congress enforcing the 15th Amendment

Question habits: Date the document first. Charts show what changed, not why. Look for cause words (because, led to, as a result). A fact can be checked; an opinion uses judgment words (best, worst, should, greatest).

stimuli.title: Timeline: Reconstruction, 1865–1877
stimuli.html:
YearEvent
1865The Civil War ends. The 13th Amendment abolishes slavery. Congress creates the Freedmen's Bureau.
1865–1866Southern state governments pass Black Codes limiting the rights of formerly enslaved people.
1867Congress passes the Reconstruction Acts, dividing most of the former Confederacy into military districts.
1868The 14th Amendment is ratified, defining citizenship and guaranteeing equal protection of the laws.
1870The 15th Amendment is ratified. Hiram Revels of Mississippi becomes the first Black U.S. senator.
1877Under the Compromise of 1877, the last federal troops are withdrawn from the South.

stimuli.title: Document 1: The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882)
stimuli.html:
Whereas in the opinion of the Government of the United States the coming of Chinese laborers to this country endangers the good order of certain localities within the territory thereof: Therefore,

Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That from and after the expiration of ninety days next after the passage of this act, and until the expiration of ten years next after the passage of this act, the coming of Chinese laborers to the United States be, and the same is hereby, suspended; and during such suspension it shall not be lawful for any Chinese laborer to come, or, having so come after the expiration of said ninety days, to remain within the United States.
stimuli.source: An Act to Execute Certain Treaty Stipulations Relating to Chinese (Chinese Exclusion Act), approved May 6, 1882, preamble and Section 1

stimuli.title: Chart: Immigrants Admitted to the United States by Decade
stimuli.html: The chart shows the number of immigrants admitted as permanent residents in each decade, in millions (rounded to the nearest tenth).
stimuli.source: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Yearbook of Immigration Statistics, Table 1 (annual figures summed by decade and rounded)

stimuli.title: Political Cartoon (described)
stimuli.html: The cartoon shows a giant octopus whose body is a large oil storage tank labeled “THE OIL TRUST.” Its long arms reach across the drawing. One arm is wrapped around a small corner grocery store, whose owner looks on helplessly. Another arm squeezes a railroad car. A third arm is coiled around the dome of a state capitol, and a fourth is stretching toward the dome of the U.S. Capitol in Washington. In the corner, a small figure labeled “THE PUBLIC” holds a newspaper with the headline “WHO RULES?”
stimuli.source: Original cartoon description written for this lesson, in the style of political cartoons published around 1900–1905

stimuli.title: Document 2: President Wilson's War Message (1917)
stimuli.html:
Background: On April 2, 1917, President Woodrow Wilson spoke to a joint session of Congress and asked it to declare war on Germany. Congress declared war four days later.

“The world must be made safe for democracy. Its peace must be planted upon the tested foundations of political liberty. We have no selfish ends to serve. We desire no conquest, no dominion. We seek no indemnities for ourselves, no material compensation for the sacrifices we shall freely make.”
stimuli.source: President Woodrow Wilson, Address to a Joint Session of Congress, April 2, 1917

stimuli.title: Document 3: Statement on Signing the Social Security Act (1935)
stimuli.html:
“This social security measure gives at least some protection to thirty millions of our citizens who will reap direct benefits through unemployment compensation, through old-age pensions and through increased services for the protection of children and the prevention of ill health.

“We can never insure one hundred percent of the population against one hundred percent of the hazards and vicissitudes of life, but we have tried to frame a law which will give some measure of protection to the average citizen and to his family against the loss of a job and against poverty-ridden old age.”

vicissitudes: unexpected changes, usually for the worse
stimuli.source: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Statement on Signing the Social Security Act, August 14, 1935

stimuli.title: Document 4: Address to Congress (1941)
stimuli.html:
“Yesterday, December 7th, 1941—a date which will live in infamy—the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan.

…

“I ask that the Congress declare that since the unprovoked and dastardly attack by Japan on Sunday, December 7th, 1941, a state of war has existed between the United States and the Japanese Empire.”

infamy: lasting shame or disgrace
stimuli.source: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Address to a Joint Session of Congress, December 8, 1941

stimuli.title: Timeline: The Cold War, 1947–1991
stimuli.html:
YearEvent
1947President Truman asks Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey to resist communist pressure (the Truman Doctrine).
1949The United States, Canada, and ten European nations form NATO, promising to defend one another.
1950U.S. troops, under the United Nations, go to defend South Korea after North Korea invades.
1957The Soviet Union launches Sputnik, the first artificial satellite.
1961East Germany builds the Berlin Wall.
1991The Soviet Union breaks apart into 15 independent countries.

stimuli.title: Document 5: Two Federal Actions Against Discrimination
stimuli.html:
Excerpt A

“It is hereby declared to be the policy of the President that there shall be equality of treatment and opportunity for all persons in the armed services without regard to race, color, religion or national origin. This policy shall be put into effect as rapidly as possible, having due regard to the time required to effectuate any necessary changes without impairing efficiency or morale.”

—Executive Order 9981, issued by President Harry S. Truman, July 26, 1948

Excerpt B

“No voting qualification or prerequisite to voting, or standard, practice, or procedure shall be imposed or applied by any State or political subdivision to deny or abridge the right of any citizen of the United States to vote on account of race or color.”

—Voting Rights Act of 1965, Section 2, passed by Congress and signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson, August 6, 1965
stimuli.source: Executive Order 9981 (1948), paragraph 1; Voting Rights Act of 1965, Section 2

items.prompt: According to the timeline, which event happened before Congress passed the Reconstruction Acts?
options: Southern state governments passed Black Codes.
The 14th Amendment was ratified.
Hiram Revels became the first Black U.S. senator.
The last federal troops were withdrawn from the South.
items.hint: Find the year of the Reconstruction Acts, then look at the rows above it.
items.explain:
The Reconstruction Acts were passed in 1867. The Black Codes were passed in 1865–1866, which is earlier.

The 14th Amendment (1868), Hiram Revels's election (1870), and the withdrawal of troops (1877) all came after 1867. A common mistake is choosing the 14th Amendment because it is close in time; check the year: 1868 comes after 1867.

items.skill: Main idea of a primary source
items.prompt: What was the main purpose of the section of the law shown in Document 1?
options: To stop Chinese laborers from coming to the United States for ten years
To allow Chinese laborers to become U.S. citizens after ninety days
To require all immigrants to the United States to pass a test
To end trade between the United States and China
items.hint: Find the word that tells what happens to "the coming of Chinese laborers."
items.explain:
The law says that "the coming of Chinese laborers to the United States be, and the same is hereby, suspended" from ninety days after passage "until the expiration of ten years." To suspend means to stop for a time. So the law stopped Chinese workers from immigrating for ten years.

The "ninety days" is only the waiting period before the ban began; the law says nothing about citizenship. It applies only to Chinese laborers, not to all immigrants, and it says nothing about trade.

items.prompt: According to the chart, how many more immigrants, in millions, were admitted in 1901–1910 than in 1931–1940?
items.hint: Read both bars, then subtract the smaller value from the larger one.
items.explain:
1901–1910: 8.8 million
1931–1940: 0.5 million
Difference: 8.8 − 0.5 = 8.3 million

A common error is using the 1921–1930 bar (4.1) instead of 1931–1940; read the labels carefully.

items.prompt: Which development best explains the low number of immigrants shown for 1931–1940?
options: The Great Depression left few jobs for newcomers, and quota laws passed in the 1920s were still limiting immigration.
The opening of Ellis Island made it harder for immigrants to enter the country.
The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 ended immigration from Europe.
The United States fought in World War II for the entire decade, so ships could not cross the ocean.
items.hint: What was happening to the U.S. economy in the 1930s? What laws about immigration had already been passed?
items.explain:
In the 1930s the Great Depression caused massive unemployment, so there were few jobs to attract immigrants, and the quota laws of 1921 and 1924 were still in force. Together they explain the drop from 4.1 million to 0.5 million.

Ellis Island opened in 1892 as an immigration station, and immigration was very high in the decades after it opened. The Chinese Exclusion Act applied to Chinese laborers, not Europeans. The United States did not enter World War II until December 1941, after this decade ended.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the cartoonist's point of view?
options: One powerful company is gaining control over small businesses, transportation, and even government.
Large oil companies help small businesses by lowering prices.
State governments are more powerful than the federal government.
Newspapers are spreading false stories about the oil industry.
items.hint: Look at what each arm of the octopus is grabbing, and at the headline the public is reading.
items.explain:
The octopus is labeled "THE OIL TRUST," and its arms squeeze a grocery store (small business), a railroad car (transportation), and a state capitol, while reaching for the U.S. Capitol (government). The headline "WHO RULES?" asks whether the trust, not the people, controls the country. The cartoonist sees the trust as a dangerous monopoly, a typical Progressive Era view.

Nothing in the cartoon suggests the trust helps anyone; the grocer looks helpless. The cartoon does not compare state and federal power, and the newspaper is shown as asking a question, not spreading falsehoods.

items.prompt: Drag each event into the era in which it took place.
choices: Upton Sinclair's The Jungle leads Congress to pass the Meat Inspection Act.
The Civilian Conservation Corps hires young men to plant trees and build trails.
The Berlin Airlift flies food and fuel into West Berlin.
Ida Tarbell publishes an investigation of Standard Oil.
President Roosevelt signs the Social Security Act.
The United States and Western European nations form NATO.
items.hint: Progressive Era: about 1890–1920. New Deal: the 1930s. Cold War: after 1945.
items.explain:
• Progressive Era: The Jungle and the Meat Inspection Act (1906); Ida Tarbell's Standard Oil investigation (published 1902–1904). Both are muckraker actions against big business.
  • New Deal: the Civilian Conservation Corps (1933) and the Social Security Act (1935). Both are Roosevelt programs responding to the Great Depression.
  • Cold War: the Berlin Airlift (1948–1949) and NATO (1949). Both were efforts to contain Soviet power.

A common mix-up is putting Social Security in the Progressive Era because it is a reform; check the date (1935) and the president (Franklin D. Roosevelt).

items.prompt: Why did President Wilson most likely include the statement "We desire no conquest, no dominion" in his address?
options: To assure Congress and the public that the United States would fight for principles, not to gain land or power
To warn Germany that the United States planned to take over German territory
To explain that the United States would remain neutral in the war
To ask Congress to pay the costs of the war with money taken from Germany
items.hint: Conquest means taking land by force; dominion means control over others. What is Wilson saying the United States does NOT want?
items.explain:
Wilson says the United States has "no selfish ends," wants "no conquest, no dominion," and seeks "no indemnities" (payments). He is presenting the war as a fight to make the world "safe for democracy," not a grab for territory or wealth. That reassures Americans that the cause is just.

He says the opposite of wanting German territory. He is asking for war, not neutrality. And "We seek no indemnities" means he is not asking for payments from Germany.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement based on Document 3.

Roosevelt says the Social Security Act will help people through unemployment compensation and {{0}}. He admits that the law {{1}}. The act is best described as part of the New Deal goal of {{2}}.

options: old-age pensions
free college tuition
guaranteed farm prices
government jobs for every citizen
cannot protect every person against every hardship
will end all poverty within ten years
covers one hundred percent of the population
replaces all state welfare programs
reform, creating a lasting system of protection against future hardship
winning World War II
breaking up monopolies
limiting immigration

items.hint: Reread the list of benefits in the first paragraph and the sentence that begins "We can never insure."
items.explain:
Blank 1: The first paragraph lists "unemployment compensation," "old-age pensions," and services for children and health. Old-age pensions is correct.

Blank 2: "We can never insure one hundred percent of the population against one hundred percent of the hazards" means the law cannot protect every person against every hardship. The choice "covers one hundred percent of the population" reverses his meaning.

Blank 3: Social Security created a permanent program to protect people against job loss and poverty in old age in the future. That is reform. Breaking up monopolies was a Progressive Era goal, and the act came six years before the United States entered World War II.

items.prompt: In Document 4, Roosevelt asks Congress, rather than acting alone, to declare that a state of war exists. Which constitutional principle explains why?
options: The Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war.
The Constitution gives the Supreme Court the power to approve all wars.
The Constitution requires the states to vote before the nation goes to war.
The Constitution allows the President to declare war only during an election year.
items.hint: Think back to Week 2: which branch has the power to declare war under Article I?
items.explain:
Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution lists the powers of Congress, including the power "To declare War." The President is commander in chief of the armed forces, but only Congress can formally declare war. That is why Roosevelt says, "I ask that the Congress declare…" Congress voted for war on Japan the same day, December 8, 1941.

The Supreme Court does not approve wars, the states do not vote on declarations of war, and no rule ties the war power to election years.

items.prompt: The U.S. Cold War policy of containment aimed to stop the spread of communism. Which events in the timeline are examples of the United States carrying out containment? Select three answers.
options: Aid to Greece and Turkey (1947)
Formation of NATO (1949)
U.S. troops defend South Korea (1950)
Launch of Sputnik (1957)
Building of the Berlin Wall (1961)
Breakup of the Soviet Union (1991)
items.hint: Look for actions the United States itself took to block communist expansion. Who carried out each of the other events?
items.explain:
• Aid to Greece and Turkey (1947): the Truman Doctrine helped those nations resist communist pressure.
  • NATO (1949): a military alliance to defend Western Europe against Soviet expansion.
  • Defending South Korea (1950): U.S. troops fought to stop communist North Korea from taking over the South.

Sputnik was launched by the Soviet Union, and the Berlin Wall was built by East Germany; neither was a U.S. action. The breakup of the Soviet Union ended the Cold War; it happened inside the Soviet Union and was not itself a U.S. containment action.

items.prompt: Read the account of the civil rights movement below. Click the sentence that states an opinion rather than a fact.
spans: On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger.
Black residents of Montgomery then boycotted the city's buses for more than a year.
In 1956, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that segregation on Montgomery's buses was unconstitutional.
The boycott was the most important protest in the history of the United States.
Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., a 26-year-old minister, was chosen to lead the Montgomery Improvement Association, which organized the boycott.
Within a decade, Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
items.hint: A fact can be checked in records. An opinion is a judgment that people could reasonably disagree with. Look for words like "best" or "most important."
items.explain:
"The boycott was the most important protest in the history of the United States" is a judgment. Historians could argue for other protests, and no record can prove it. That makes it an opinion.

Every other sentence can be checked: the date and place of Parks's arrest, the length of the boycott, the 1956 Supreme Court ruling, King's role as a leader, and the dates of the 1964 and 1965 laws.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes a difference between Excerpt A and Excerpt B?
options: Excerpt A is an order from the President about the armed forces, while Excerpt B is a law passed by Congress about voting.
Excerpt A bans discrimination only on account of race, while Excerpt B also bans discrimination on account of religion.
Excerpt A applies to state governments, while Excerpt B applies only to the federal government.
Excerpt A was a Supreme Court ruling, while Excerpt B was a constitutional amendment.
items.hint: Check the source line under each excerpt: who issued it, and what area of life does it cover?
items.explain:
Excerpt A is Executive Order 9981, issued by President Truman, and it covers "all persons in the armed services." Excerpt B is Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, a law passed by Congress, and it covers "the right…to vote." So they differ in both who acted and what area they cover, even though both target discrimination.

The religion option reverses the documents: Excerpt A lists "race, color, religion or national origin," while Excerpt B lists only "race or color." Excerpt B is the one aimed at "any State or political subdivision." Neither excerpt is a court ruling or an amendment.
